lesson.title: Entfernung: die Nähe, weit, fern, quer, entlang
lesson.subtitle: near and far on one axis — and the two words that walk a path instead of pointing at a place

hook.title: One Axis: Nah to Fern
hook.content: Distance in German is one line with two ends. die Nähe holds the near end: German nah and English nigh are the same ancient word, *nēhwaz — and English even kept the comparison: near was originally nigh's comparative, 'nigher', frozen into its own word. weit ↔ wide is a pure twin, *wīdaz, the same sound in both languages: when German asks Wie weit ist es? it is literally asking how WIDE the gap is. fern ↔ far share the ancient beyond-root; English drifted to far, German kept fern — and built das Fernsehen, the far-seer, on it. Then the two path words: entlang is ent + lang, and lang ↔ long is a pure twin — German names the path first and hangs entlang behind it: den Fluss entlang. quer is the cross-word; English queer may even be its borrowing [UNVERIFIED — check]. Nah, die Nähe, weit, fern — and two words for the shape of the road between.

footnotes.title: wie weit, never wie fern
footnotes.content: German asks distance with wie weit — 'how wide' — and never with fern. fern states a fact from where you stand (der Strand ist nicht fern), while weit measures the stretch between two points. The question is wide; the answer is far.

pattern.title: Asking, Answering, Crossing, Walking
pattern.content: Ask the stretch: Wie weit ist es? Answer with time, not numbers: Zehn Minuten zu Fuß. State remoteness: Der Weg ist nicht fern. Locate with die Nähe: in der Nähe — In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt. Cross the space: quer durch die Stadt — durch does the case work. Walk the path: Wir gehen den Fluss entlang — the path takes accusative (den Fluss) and entlang stands AFTER it, the opposite of English word order.
pattern.linguist_note: English split the old near-family three ways: nigh retreated into poetry, near took the daily slot, and nearly drifted into 'almost'. German kept one adjective, nah, and one noun, die Nähe — the family never had to split.

exercises.prompt: The near-far axis and the two path words — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.german: In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt
Ich fahre quer durch die Stadt

matching_pairs.english: Half of the street is new
matching_pairs.german: Die Hälfte der Straße ist neu

matching_pairs.english: We take a detour — the way is far
matching_pairs.german: Wir nehmen einen Umweg, der Weg ist weit

matching_pairs.english: Go straight ahead to the corner
matching_pairs.german: Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ecke

matching_pairs.english: From north to south it is far
matching_pairs.german: Von Norden bis Süden ist es weit

matching_pairs.english: In the west is the sea, in the east the city
matching_pairs.german: Im Westen ist das Meer, im Osten die Stadt

exercises.target_answer: Wie weit ist der Strand?, Der Weg ist nicht fern, In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt, Ich fahre quer durch die Stadt, Zehn Minuten zu Fuß, Die Hälfte der Straße ist neu, Wir nehmen einen Umweg, der Weg ist weit, Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ecke, Von Norden bis Süden ist es weit, Im Westen ist das Meer, im Osten die Stadt
exercises.meaning: how far, not far, nearby, across, on foot, half
exercises.explanation: wie weit asks the stretch, fern states the remoteness, die Nähe names the neighborhood, and quer durch crosses the space. Time answers where numbers fail: Zehn Minuten zu Fuß.

exercises.prompt: 'Wie _____ ist der Weg?' — which word does German use to ask HOW FAR?
exercises.meaning: wie weit = how far — the wide-word asks the distance
exercises.explanation: The fixed question is wie weit — literally 'how wide', the twin of wide at work. fern answers, it never asks: der Weg ist nicht fern. And eins and vier count things, not kilometers.

exercises.prompt: 'weit' is a pure twin — the same ancient *wīdaz. Which English word is it?
exercises.meaning: weit ↔ wide: same sound, same root, same width
exercises.explanation: weit and wide are one word in two mouths: *wīdaz. white is the twin of a different German word (weiß), and with and wit come from other roots entirely — the width belongs to weit.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the time-answer frame: 'I wait four minutes'
exercises.explanation: German answers distance in time: not four streets but four minutes. warte takes the time phrase with no preposition — the same accusative frame as Ich warte zehn Minuten from the numbers lesson.
entlang rides BEHIND the path: den Fluss entlang, never entlang den Fluss. The path takes accusative — den, not dem — which is why dem sits in the bank as the trap tile.

summary.outcome: Ask wie weit, answer with fern or a time, and shape the path with quer and entlang.

use_example.german: Wie weit ist der Strand? — Zehn Minuten zu Fuß.
use_example.english: How far is the beach? — Ten minutes on foot.

summary.takeaway: die Nähe ↔ nigh, weit ↔ wide, fern ↔ far, entlang = ent + lang — one axis, two path words, and entlang always last.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the words English handed over — Sofa, Radio, Klavier, Computer, Kino.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Entfernung: die Nähe, weit, fern, quer, entlang (We walk along the river):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir gehen den Fluss entlang" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Entfernung: die Nähe, weit, fern, quer, entlang without relying on short-term echo.

nähe.context_phrase: In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt.
nähe.etymology_derivation: nah + -e; nah is the twin of archaic English nigh. [wiktionary]

weit.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīdaz — the direct cognate of English wide. [wiktionary]

fern.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ferrai — the same word as English far (see der Fernseher, far-seer). [wiktionary]

quer.context_phrase: Der Baum liegt quer über dem Weg.
quer.context_translation: The tree lies across the path.
quer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *þwerh, oblique (Old High German twerh); etymonline lists German quer as a cognate of English thwart, from Old Norse þverr, across. [wiktionary][etymonline]

entlang.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, essentially in lang — the lang element is the twin of English long, so it works just like along. [wiktionary]

norden.context_translation: In the north it often rains.
norden.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from Nord, the twin of north; used with im for in the north. [wiktionary]

osten.context_phrase: Der Wind kommt aus dem Osten.
osten.context_translation: The wind comes from the east.
osten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą — the same root as English east, ultimately from the dawn root *ausos, as in Latin aurora. [wiktionary]

westen.context_phrase: Die Sonne geht im Westen unter.
westen.context_translation: The sun sets in the west.
westen.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from West, the twin of west; used with im for in the west. [wiktionary]

süden.context_phrase: Im Süden ist die Sonne stärker.
süden.context_translation: In the south the sun is stronger.
süden.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German süden, ultimately Proto-Germanic *sunþanē — the old noun *sunþrą gave both English south and German Süd (th → d). [wiktionary]

straße.etymology_derivation: Roman paved road (via strata) gave English "street" (kept Latin "t") and German "Straße" (shifted "t" to sharp "ß").

fluss.context_phrase: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
fluss.context_translation: The river flows through the city.
fluss.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German vluȥ, from Proto-Germanic *flutiz, from the same root as fließen, to flow. English flow is the cognate of that root. [wiktionary]

strand.context_translation: We are going to the beach.
strand.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *strando — the page lists English strand (shore) as the direct cognate, as in London's Strand. [wiktionary]

umweg.context_phrase: Wir nehmen einen Umweg wegen der Baustelle.
umweg.context_translation: We take a detour because of the construction site.
umweg.etymology_derivation: um + Weg, from Middle High German umbe, around, plus wec, way; Weg is the documented twin of way — an around-way, a detour. [wiktionary]

geradeaus.context_phrase: Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ecke.
geradeaus.context_translation: Go straight ahead to the corner.
geradeaus.etymology_derivation: gerade + aus fused into one adverb; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

eins.context_translation: I have only one of those.
eins.etymology_derivation: Contraction of eines, Proto-Germanic *ainaz — the twin of English one (see ein). [wiktionary]

vier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *feuwar — the direct twin of English four. [wiktionary]

zehn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *tehun — the twin of English ten with the classic t → z shift. [wiktionary]

hälfte.context_phrase: Ich esse nur die Hälfte des Kuchens.
hälfte.context_translation: I eat only half of the cake.
hälfte.etymology_derivation: halb + the deadjectival suffix -te — the twin of half; the entry notes the old b ↔ ft alternation was never levelled. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
